study.title: PSR J0653+0443: An Eclipsing Millisecond Pulsar in an Extremely Eccentric Double Neutron Star System

cover.headline: An extremely warped orbit could mean **binary stars collide more unpredictably** than models allow

slides.title: If this orbit survived, current models may badly underestimate how many colliding neutron stars we are missing.
slides.body:
Astronomers use star evolution models to predict how many neutron star pairs exist and what their orbits look like. This system was predicted to occur less than once in two hundred discoveries.

Finding it suggests the models undercount rare orbits. That matters for gravitational wave searches.

slides.title: The team reports a neutron star pair in an orbit with eccentricity 0.992, circling once every 79 days.
slides.body:
A perfect circle has eccentricity zero. This is among the most elongated orbits ever recorded for a neutron star binary.

The pulsar swings past at 1.14 million meters per second, then coasts out slowly.

slides.title: The extreme stretch can only come from a violent kick when the second star exploded as a supernova.
slides.body:
When a massive star collapses, the newborn neutron star can be flung at high speed. A large, mistimed kick warps the orbit drastically.

The probability of detecting a system like this is less than 0.005, challenging current evolution theory.

caveats: This is a preprint. It has not been peer reviewed, so no independent expert has checked the work yet.
The detection probability estimate depends on existing models, which this discovery itself calls into question.
The system is inferred from pulsar timing data. Direct imaging of the neutron stars is not possible at this distance.

source.abstract: Double neutron star (DNS) systems emit gravitational waves (GW) as they orbit each other, with waveforms dependent on their orbital properties \cite{Poisson+2014grav.book.....P}. The number of DNS systems surviving binary star evolution in the Milky Way and the distribution of their orbital parameters are fundamental questions for GW astronomy and binary evolution studies. Here, we report the discovery of a new Galactic field DNS system, PSR J0653+0443, comprising two ~1.4 $M_\odot$ components in an extremely eccentric orbit $e=0.992387$, $P_{\rm orb}=79.084$ d. Its unique orbital dynamics include a 46-minute transit from true anomaly $θ=-90^\circ$ to $90^\circ$ and striking periastron relative motion (maximum acceleration 1.11~km~s$^{-2}$, peak speed 1.14$\times$10$^6$~m~s$^{-1}$. The pulsar undergoes an 85-second conjunction eclipse, indicating a nearly edge-on binary orbit. Short-term variations in the periastron advance induce significant pulse arrival time modulation spanning -2.91 to +2.49 ms --- at least an order of magnitude larger than that observed in any other DNS system. From this modulation, the non-relativistic periastron advance rate is constrained to $-1.5^{+0.9}_{-0.8}\times10^{-4}$ deg yr$^{-1}$. The extreme orbital eccentricity can only be attributed to a large kick velocity imparted during the iron-core collapse supernova of the progenitor of the second component. The predicted detection probability of such a PSR J0653+0443-like DNS system is $\lesssim 5 \times 10^{-3}$, implying that our discovery of this system challenges current understanding of binary evolution. This extraordinary DNS system emits periodic gravitational wave bursts, with the GW energy flux peaking at 0.357 mHz. This makes it an ideal target for the future LISAmax mission.
